## Summary

This change restores the expected default behavior for non-`codex_apps` MCP tools in `auto` approval mode when the server does not provide usable risk annotations.

Custom MCP servers may omit `ToolAnnotations` entirely, or they may emit an "empty" `ToolAnnotations` object where every hint is `None`. Both cases should behave the same way: Codex should treat the tool as lacking annotation data, not route it into the app-tool approval path.

Addresses #15824
Addresses #16685

For non-`codex_apps` MCP tools in the default `auto` approval mode:

- Missing annotations skip the approval path.
- Empty annotations (all hints `None`) also skip the approval path.
- Explicit `prompt` mode still prompts.
- Explicit `approve` mode still uses the allow/ARC path.
- `codex_apps` behavior is unchanged.

## Summary

This PR fixes the Codex-side failure modes that were preventing `spawn_agents_on_csv` from behaving like a real high-concurrency fanout primitive and from returning control cleanly to callers.

It now addresses six linked problems:

1. CSV fanout startup underfilled badly because worker creation was serialized.
2. Scheduler slots stayed occupied after rows were already completed in SQLite.
3. Agent-job shutdown could lose track of live worker threads during teardown.
4. `turn/completed` notifications could arrive without the terminal turn items that `exec` needed for clean shutdown.
5. `codex exec` could hang forever after the root turn completed because it performed an unbounded `thread/read` backfill on the same backpressured in-process event pipeline.
6. Under shared `agents.max_threads` pressure, `AgentLimitReached` could turn into a hot retry loop against `spawn_agent`, SQLite, and logging instead of backing off and waiting for capacity.

## User-visible impact

Before this PR:

- `spawn_agents_on_csv(max_concurrency=64)` could sustain only a small fraction of the requested concurrency.
- Rows could be marked completed in state while the scheduler still treated their workers as busy.
- Some agent-job runs finished the underlying work but failed to return control promptly.
- End-to-end wrappers such as `security_audit` could hang after `task_complete`, never producing their final report files.
- Under shared-capacity contention, fanout could churn locally instead of waiting for slots to free.

After this PR:

- worker startup fills toward the requested concurrency instead of serially trickling
- scheduler slots are reclaimed when the DB says rows are no longer running
- agent-job teardown preserves tracking long enough for later cleanup to reap workers correctly
- app-server includes terminal turn items in `turn/completed`
- post-turn `exec` shutdown no longer blocks forever on a backfill `thread/read`
- fanout backs off instead of hot-retrying when global agent slots are full
- the Firefox `security_audit` repros now complete end-to-end and write both markdown and HTML reports

## Root causes

### 1. Serialized worker bring-up in agent jobs

`spawn_agents_on_csv` used to refill by looping pending items and `await`ing a full `spawn_agent(...)` for each one before moving to the next. Because `spawn_agent(...)` waits through child session bring-up until `SessionConfigured`, refill throughput was limited by worker startup latency rather than by the requested concurrency.

### 2. DB completion and scheduler occupancy diverged

`report_agent_job_result` committed row completion immediately, but the in-memory scheduler only freed the corresponding slot later when the worker session itself reached a terminal state. That let rows be completed in SQLite while still consuming fanout capacity.

### 3. Teardown untracked workers too early

The slot-reclamation shutdown path released scheduler capacity by calling a shutdown helper that also removed the worker from `ThreadManager` immediately. That made capacity accounting look better, but it could leave a still-running worker no longer visible to later cleanup.

### 4. Terminal turn payloads were not reliably attached to `turn/completed`

`exec` wants the final turn items when it handles `TurnCompleted`. In large fanout runs, app-server could emit `turn/completed` with an empty terminal snapshot, which forced `exec` into a late `thread/read` backfill during shutdown.

### 5. `exec` did an unbounded backfill request after `TurnCompleted`

When `exec` receives `TurnCompleted`, it backfills missing turn items with a `thread/read`. In large fanout runs, the in-process event stream can still be under heavy backpressure. Because the backfill request shared the same bounded pipeline, `exec` could wait forever on `thread/read` while the worker was blocked trying to forward must-deliver completion events.

### 6. `AgentLimitReached` counted as “progress” instead of “wait”

The parallel startup path requeued blocked items back to `Pending`, but that still looked like scheduler progress to the main loop. Under shared `agents.max_threads` contention, the loop could immediately try the same refill again instead of waiting for a real worker/status change.

## What changed

### Parallel startup and stronger refill behavior

- Parallelized CSV worker startup in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/agent_jobs.rs` and `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/agent_jobs_startup.rs`.
- Added tracking for both `active_items` and `starting_items` so refill now targets `active + starting == max_concurrency`.
- Startup now claims rows in state first, then completes assignment when the worker actually comes up.
- Added startup instrumentation so logs show queued launches, startup latency, and effective concurrency.

### Scheduler slot reclamation and terminal-state reconciliation

- Added explicit slot reconciliation in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/agent_jobs_slots.rs`.
- Refill now trusts terminal DB state instead of waiting only on in-memory worker finalization.
- Workers that report successfully no longer hold scheduler slots hostage while they continue draining.
- Added logging that shows both DB and scheduler views of running work.

### Correctness fixes around shutdown and cancellation

- Preserved thread tracking during shutdown in `codex-rs/core/src/agent/control.rs` so releasing a slot does not also hide a still-live worker from later teardown.
- Added coverage for the preserved-tracking shutdown behavior in `codex-rs/core/src/agent/control_tests.rs`.
- Made result reporting and `stop=true` cancellation state updates atomic in `codex-rs/state/src/runtime/agent_jobs.rs`.
- Kept agent-job semantics intact around state assignment, failure handling, and max-thread limits.

### Turn-completion and exec-shutdown fixes

- App-server now retains the terminal turn snapshot and attaches it directly to `turn/completed` instead of relying on a late best-effort read.
- `exec` still keeps a bounded fallback `thread/read`, but it now times out and continues shutdown instead of hanging forever.
- Added targeted app-server / protocol / exec coverage for the turn-completion payload and bounded backfill behavior.

### Backoff when global agent slots are exhausted

- Startup draining now returns structured state (`progressed` plus `agent_limit_reached`) instead of only a boolean.
- The main agent-job loop now treats `AgentLimitReached` as a blocked refill condition.
- When fanout is locally ready to launch but global `agents.max_threads` is full, the loop stops relaunching immediately and waits for a startup or status change before retrying.
- Added targeted tests for both the wait decision and the `AgentLimitReached -> Pending` requeue path.

## Validation

### Automated validation

Ran the following locally during development:

- `cargo test -p codex-state report_agent_job_item_result_and_cancel_job_is_atomic`
- `cargo test -p codex-core spawn_agents_on_csv -- --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p codex-core request_live_agent_shutdown_preserving_thread_releases_slot_without_untracking -- --nocapture`
- `cargo test -p codex-core should_wait_when_agent_limit_blocks_refill`
- `cargo test -p codex-core drain_ready_startups_reports_agent_limit_and_requeues_item`
- `cargo test -p codex-exec`
- `cargo test -p codex-app-server test_handle_turn_complete_emits_completed_without_error`
- `cargo test -p codex-app-server-protocol`
- `just fmt`
- `just fix -p codex-core`
- `just fix -p codex-state`
- `just fix -p codex-exec`
- `just fix -p codex-app-server`
- `just fix -p codex-app-server-protocol`

Per repo guidance, I did not run the full workspace `cargo test` without explicit approval.

### Synthetic fanout validation

The synthetic CSV fanout repro reached the requested concurrency instead of serially trickling worker creation. Startup logs showed fanout filling to the target and sustaining materially higher live-worker counts than before.

### End-to-end Firefox validation

Re-ran the real `security_audit` Firefox repros against this branch’s `target/debug/codex` binary.

Successful runs included:

- `netwerk/base`
  - `337` rows processed
  - `0` failures
  - generated `assess_output.csv`, `report.md`, and `report.html`
- `ipc/glue`
  - `162` rows processed
  - `0` failures
  - generated `assess_output.csv`, `report.md`, and `report.html`

These runs returned control to the shell instead of hanging after `task_complete`.

## Remaining caveat

Heavy fanout still produces `in-process app-server event stream lagged; dropped ... events` warnings under load. Those warnings reflect real backpressure, but the critical completion path is now robust enough that the run finishes end-to-end instead of hanging.

## Commit structure

This branch now contains five commits:

- `ab9f9848c7` Parallelize CSV agent job startup
- `dac04fba7e` Reclaim agent-job fanout slots after report
- `1f57fd56fa` Finish agent-job fanout completion and exec shutdown
- `ff98e9ac70` Include terminal items in turn completion events
- `4861584e9d` Back off CSV fanout when agent slots are full

## Summary

This PR adds release files that are made for the standalone installer.

This PR publishes those files during the Rust release:

- `codex-standalone-<platform>-<version>.tar.gz`
- `codex-installer_SHA256SUMS`

Each standalone archive has the layout the installer needs directly. It contains `codex`, `rg`, and the Windows helper binaries where needed.

## Stack

1. #18910, this PR: publish standalone installer archives and their checksum file.
2. #18901: make the Unix and Windows installers download those archives and verify them before install.

## Design decisions

- Checksum generation stays as its own release step. The archive-staging script's job is to produce standalone archives. The checksum step's job is to publish a manifest over the final set of release archives that actually landed in `dist/installer`.
- The installer consumes one checksum manifest for the release instead of per-archive embedded metadata. This keeps the installer flow simple: download `codex-installer_SHA256SUMS`, look up the requested archive, verify it, then extract it.
- This follows the checksum-manifest pattern we already use for `rusty_v8`: stage artifacts, write a SHA-256 manifest next to them, and have consumers verify downloads against that manifest.

## Tests

Tests: workflow formatter check, Python compile checks, standalone archive staging smoke tests covering linux-x64, linux-arm64, darwin-x64, darwin-arm64, win32-x64, and win32-arm64 via synthetic vendor inputs, plus archive content checks for Unix and Windows layouts.

## Why

Browser Use and Computer Use approvals can arrive as MCP `elicitation/create` requests. When Guardian/auto-review is enabled, approval-shaped elicitations should be reviewed before they become user prompts, the same way other approval surfaces can be reviewed. Without this routing, connector approvals that are represented as MCP elicitations bypass the auto-review path and remain a manual prompt even in configurations intended to delegate approval review.

## What changed

- Added an optional MCP elicitation reviewer hook in `codex-mcp` that can resolve an elicitation before the normal prompt event is emitted.
- Wired Codex sessions to route approval-shaped MCP form elicitations through Guardian when the current turn is configured for auto-review.
- Kept the routing intentionally narrow: only empty-schema form elicitations are eligible for Guardian review. URL elicitations and forms that require user-provided content still use the existing user prompt path.
- Added a `McpElicitation` Guardian action across analytics, protocol, app-server v2, and generated schema fixtures so app clients can render/replay the review lifecycle.
- Added regression coverage for reviewer resolution before prompt emission and the Guardian JSON payload shape.

## Review notes

The Guardian decision mapping for MCP elicitations accepts ordinary approve/session-approve decisions, declines denial/timeouts, cancels aborts, and fails closed for unrelated amendment-style decisions. That keeps this boundary from accidentally treating exec-policy or network-policy amendments as valid MCP elicitation answers.

## Why

`codex-core` currently owns prompt construction, sampling retries, and much of the model/tool loop orchestration alongside concrete local tool implementations. That makes it hard to identify which parts of the agent loop are truly core orchestration concerns versus host-specific execution details.

This draft PR is a proof of concept for extracting a smaller `codex-kernel` crate and making those seams explicit. The goal here is less “final API polish” and more “can this boundary carry the existing app-server behavior without breaking the system?”

- Added a new `codex-kernel` workspace crate in `codex-rs/kernel`.
- Moved prompt construction and the retryable outer sampling loop into `codex-kernel`.
- Split model-visible tool registration out of prompt config into an explicit `ToolConfig`.

- Moved the default “model emitted a tool call, attempt the complementary output item” behavior into `codex-kernel`, rather than leaving that policy entirely inside `codex-core`.

This is intentionally a seam-finding PoC. The main thing it tries to answer is whether the sampling loop and tool loop can be moved behind host-provided traits without dragging more `codex-core` implementation detail into the new crate.

## Summary

- Decode backslash escapes in unquoted Bash/Zsh words before command-safety matching, so shell-escaped tokens such as `-e\xec` are evaluated as the argv Bash will actually execute.
- Require approval when a command requests a sandbox override and the executable is an explicit path inside a sandbox-writable location, preventing basename-safe paths like `/tmp/cat` from bypassing review.
- Suppress execpolicy amendment suggestions for those sandbox-writable executable paths.

## Root Cause

Two approval bypasses came from comparing the wrong executable surface:

- Bash parser safety checks used raw tree-sitter word text, while Bash removes unquoted backslash escapes before execution.

- Treat managed profiles as `workspace-write` only when the active `cwd` is writable; explicit write roots outside `cwd` now summarize as `custom permissions`.

items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #19753 after investigating reports of stale MCP server processes and app-server logs like `Failed to terminate MCP process group`.

`mcpServerStatus/list` is declared as a globally serialized RPC, but the handler was spawning the actual MCP inventory work into a detached task and returning immediately. That let multiple status-list requests overlap outside the serialization queue and connection RPC gate, with each request able to create a temporary `McpConnectionManager` and start MCP clients. Similar detached-task behavior existed for app-server MCP resource reads and tool calls, which could keep thread/MCP state alive after the original RPC handler was considered complete.

This change keeps the MCP work inside the request future so the existing serialization and connection lifecycle tracking actually cover it.

## Changes

- Await `mcpServerStatus/list`, `mcpServer/resource/read`, and `mcpServer/tool/call` work directly in the app-server RPC handlers instead of detaching it with `tokio::spawn`.
- Explicitly shut down temporary MCP managers used by threadless resource reads and status snapshots after their work completes.
- Harden stdio MCP process termination so local termination failures are surfaced, keep the process handle retryable, and report failed `taskkill` status on Windows.
- Add a regression test proving overlapping `mcpServerStatus/list` requests do not run concurrent inventory work.

## Why

This is another small step in the SandboxPolicy -> PermissionProfile migration. The Windows sandbox still has several legacy-policy-shaped internals. This PR isolates one of them by moving the workspace-write allow/deny path calculation behind a policy-free helper, while keeping the existing `compute_allow_paths()` legacy wrapper for current callers.

That keeps behavior unchanged today but makes the allow-path calculation easier to reuse from `PermissionProfile`/runtime-permission inputs in a later PR without constructing a `SandboxPolicy` just to reach this code.

## What Changed

- Adds a `WorkspaceWriteAllowPathInputs` helper shape that carries only the data the allow-path calculation actually needs: policy cwd, command cwd, env map, writable roots, and whether TEMP/TMP roots should be included.
- Keeps `compute_allow_paths()` as the compatibility adapter from `SandboxPolicy::WorkspaceWrite` to that helper.
- Updates allow-path unit tests to exercise the policy-free helper directly instead of constructing `SandboxPolicy` fixtures.
- Preserves the existing behavior for protected subdirectories: existing `.git`, `.codex`, and `.agents` entries under writable roots are denied, and missing protected subdirectories are not materialized into deny paths.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p codex-windows-sandbox --tests`
- `just fix -p codex-windows-sandbox`

items.body:
## Why

Windows release builds are currently expensive enough that the Windows jobs can dominate release latency. This PR is a proof of concept for building Windows release binaries from Linux with Cargo, using `cargo-xwin` to target `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.

The goal is to validate whether Cargo-based cross compilation can build the Windows release binaries we care about before changing the real signed release workflow. This PoC intentionally does not include signing logic.

## What Changed

Adds `.github/workflows/rust-release-windows-cross-compile-poc.yml`, a minimal workflow that:

- runs on `ubuntu-24.04`
- installs the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` Rust target
- installs `cargo-xwin`
- caches Cargo registry/git data plus the xwin MSVC CRT and Windows SDK cache
- builds these release binaries:
  - `codex-responses-api-proxy`
  - `codex-app-server`
  - `codex`
- verifies that the outputs are Windows `PE32+` executables
- uploads the binaries and Cargo timing HTML as workflow artifacts

## Toolchain Confidence

This PoC is still a Cargo-based release build: the workflow runs `cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`. It is not a Bazel build, and it is not changing the Rust target ABI away from the normal Windows MSVC target.

The important distinction from a native Windows `cargo build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` is the host toolchain around Cargo:

- native Windows builds typically use MSVC `link.exe`, an installed Visual Studio toolchain, and the installed Windows SDK
- `cargo-xwin` uses `xwin` to provide the Microsoft CRT and Windows SDK headers/libs on non-Windows hosts
- the cross build uses LLVM tooling, including `lld-link`; `cargo-xwin` defaults C/C++ cross-compilation to `clang-cl`

This is why the PoC verifies the produced files are normal Windows `PE32+` executables for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.

For linker maturity, this is not an obscure linker path. LLVM's Windows `lld` documentation says `lld-link` accepts almost all `link.exe` command-line options and is used to link production Windows builds of large real-world binaries such as Firefox and Chromium:

https://lld.llvm.org/windows_support.html

That does **not** mean Firefox or Chromium use `cargo-xwin`; the relevant point is that the linker family used by this cross-compilation path is already used for major production Windows binaries.

Relevant tool docs:

- `cargo-xwin`: https://github.com/rust-cross/cargo-xwin
- `xwin`: https://github.com/Jake-Shadle/xwin
- LLVM `lld-link`: https://lld.llvm.org/windows_support.html

Before replacing the signed release path, we should still smoke-test the cross-built binaries on Windows and compare any relevant startup/runtime benchmarks. The main risks are compatibility or behavioral differences from `lld-link`, `clang-cl`, or SDK/CRT version differences, not a known systematic Rust runtime performance penalty from cross-compilation itself.

## Workflow Commands

I triggered the successful thin-LTO workflow by pushing updates to the draft PR branch:

```shell
sl pr submit -d
```

That used the workflow's `pull_request` trigger.

I triggered the fat-LTO experiment with:

```shell
gh workflow run rust-release-windows-cross-compile-poc.yml \
  --repo openai/codex \
  --ref pr20485 \
  -f release_lto=fat
```

The build commands executed by the workflow are:

```shell
cargo xwin build \
  --release \
  --target "$WINDOWS_TARGET" \
  --timings \
  --bin codex-responses-api-proxy

cargo xwin build \
  --release \
  --target "$WINDOWS_TARGET" \
  --timings \
  --bin codex-app-server

cargo xwin build \
  --release \
  --target "$WINDOWS_TARGET" \
  --timings \
  --bin codex
```

For both successful runs, `WINDOWS_TARGET` was `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`.

## Verification

Successful thin-LTO workflow run:

https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25185982350

Successful thin-LTO job:

https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25185982350/job/73843273846

Per-binary build step timing from the successful thin-LTO run:

- `codex-responses-api-proxy`: 1m59s
- `codex-app-server`: 23m01s
- `codex`: 16m03s
- total job time: about 42m11s

Successful fat-LTO workflow run:

https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25190714066

Successful fat-LTO job:

https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25190714066/job/73859747064

Per-binary build step timing from the successful fat-LTO run:

- `codex-responses-api-proxy`: 1m59s
- `codex-app-server`: 25m01s
- `codex`: 23m58s
- total job time: about 54m30s

These are the durations of each sequential `cargo xwin build` step. Later build steps benefit from dependencies and artifacts produced by earlier steps in the same job.

The workflow verified these output files:

- `target/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/release/codex-responses-api-proxy.exe`
- `target/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/release/codex-app-server.exe`
- `target/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/release/codex.exe`

## Downloading The Binaries

From the GitHub web UI:

1. Open the workflow run:
   - thin LTO: https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25185982350
   - fat LTO: https://github.com/openai/codex/actions/runs/25190714066
2. Scroll to the bottom of the run page.
3. In **Artifacts**, click `windows-cross-compile-poc-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-primary-app-server`.

GitHub downloads the artifact as a `.zip`. You must be logged into GitHub and have access to the repo.

From the CLI:

```shell
gh run download 25185982350 \
  --repo openai/codex \
  --name windows-cross-compile-poc-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-primary-app-server

gh run download 25190714066 \
  --repo openai/codex \
  --name windows-cross-compile-poc-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-primary-app-server
```

Each artifact contains:

- `codex.exe`
- `codex-app-server.exe`
- `codex-responses-api-proxy.exe`

Both artifacts expire on 2026-07-29.

## Why

Threads are eligible for unload after the last connection unsubscribes, but the appropriate grace period depends on the connection type. Local in-process and stdio clients can release immediately after the last subscriber leaves, while socket, TCP websocket, and remote-control clients should keep the existing 30-minute grace window to preserve reconnect behavior.

## What changed

- Added per-origin unload delays on `ConnectionOrigin`.
- Carried each initialized connection delay into app-server thread subscription state.
- Made `ThreadStateManager` publish whether subscribers exist plus the winning unload delay, using the maximum delay among active subscribers and retaining that value once the thread becomes idle.
- Passed distinct unix socket and websocket origins through transport setup.
- Updated v2 unsubscribe tests and README notes for immediate stdio unload behavior.
